findings.claim: Stem: 'Austria's vineyard classification is being written privately before it is written into law'; exp: 'The state's own contribution is the Riedenwein tier, which protects the site name but ranks nothing ... the law only guarantees that the name on the bottle is a real vineyard.'
findings.because: Since the Weinrecht-Sammelverordnung 2023 (August 2023, signed by Agriculture Minister Totschnig), Austrian wine law defines 'Erste Lage' and 'Große Lage'. It reserves both terms for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, with lower maximum yields and hand harvest. Regional wine committees propose the classifications, and a site can become Große Lage no sooner than five years after Erste Lage. First statutory classifications were expected from the 2025 vintage. The ÖTW model was written into law, so the law now does rank sites and the claim that it ranks nothing is out of date.
findings.fix: Stem: 'Austria's private vineyard classifications preceded the legal one. Which association classified Erste Lage sites along the Danube, and which classifies Erste STK Ried and Grosse STK Ried in Styria?' Replace the last exp sentence with: 'Since the Weinrecht-Sammelverordnung 2023, the law itself provides Erste Lage and Große Lage tiers for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, proposed by the regional wine committees on the ÖTW model (Große Lage no sooner than five years after Erste Lage; first statutory classifications from the 2025 vintage at the earliest).' Keep the ÖTW and STK answers.
findings.verifyReason: The finding holds. The Weinrecht-Sammelverordnung 2023 added a chapter to Austrian labelling law that creates two legal site tiers, "Erste Lage" and "Große Lage". Both terms are reserved for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, and only in regions whose DAC already has the three levels Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein. The classified wines need lower maximum yields and hand harvest. A Ried can become Große Lage no sooner than five years after it became Erste Lage. The Regional Wine Committee starts the process and the National Wine Committee approves it. So the explanation's line that the state's Riedenwein tier "ranks nothing" and that "the law only guarantees that the name on the bottle is a real vineyard" has been out of date since 2023. The keyed answers (ÖTW for the Danube, STK for Styria) are still correct. The original stem is still defensible, because as of the 2024 reporting no region had actually classified any site under the law. The private classifications are still the working ones, and the legal framework is only an offer to the regions. The examiner's fix needs one correction. It says the first statutory classifications come "from the 2025 vintage at the earliest", but the sources only say that no classifications were expected before 2025 (a calendar year, not a vintage). The fix should also say that the National Wine Committee gives final approval.
findings.finalFix: Stem: "Austria's vineyard classifications were written privately before the law made room for one. Which association classifies Erste Lage sites in the Danube regions, and which classifies Erste STK Ried and Grosse STK Ried in Styria?" Keep the accepted answers (ÖTW, STK). Replace the exp from "The state's own contribution..." onward with: "The Riedenwein tier on its own only protects the site name. Since the Weinrecht-Sammelverordnung 2023, however, the law provides two ranked tiers, Erste Lage and Große Lage. They are reserved for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, and only in regions whose DAC has the Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein levels. They require lower yields and hand harvest. The Regional Wine Committee proposes the sites and the National Wine Committee approves them, and a Ried can become Große Lage no sooner than five years after it became Erste Lage. No statutory classification was expected before 2025, so in practice the working hierarchy is still the associations' own, largely on the ÖTW model."

question.q: Austria's vineyard classification is being written privately before it is written into law. Which association classifies Erste Lage sites in the Danube regions, and which classifies Erste STK Ried and Grosse STK Ried in Styria?
accept: otw osterreichische traditionsweinguter and stk steirische terroir und klassikweinguter
otw for the danube, stk for styria
osterreichische traditionsweinguter and the styrian stk growers
otw erste lage and stk steirische terroir klassikweinguter
question.ans: The ÖTW (Österreichische Traditionsweingüter) along the Danube, and the STK (Steirische Terroir- und Klassikweingüter) in Steiermark
question.exp: Both are private growers' associations on the VDP model, not INAO-style law: ÖTW began classifying Erste Lage sites in Kamptal and Kremstal in 2010 and spread to Traisental, Wagram, Carnuntum and Wien, marking approved sites with its 1ÖTW logo; STK runs a pyramid rising to Grosse STK Ried. The state's own contribution is the Riedenwein tier, which protects the site name but ranks nothing — the takeaway is that in Austria the hierarchy of sites is association work, and the law only guarantees that the name on the bottle is a real vineyard.

findings.claim: Stem asks for 'one benchmark for bitter-orange Milanese style'; answer 'e.g., Ramazzotti/Averna (dark), Montenegro (floral), Campari the aperitivo pole' and accept list 'digestivo averna montenegro campari ramazzotti' / 'digestif bitter liqueur'
findings.because: Only Ramazzotti (first made in Milan in 1815) and Campari (Milan) are Milanese. Averna is made in Caltanissetta, Sicily (1868), and Montenegro in Bologna (1885). The keyed answer pairs Averna with Ramazzotti as if both were the Milanese benchmark. The accept list would credit Averna or Montenegro, or even a generic 'digestif bitter liqueur', as the Milanese benchmark the stem asks for.
findings.fix: Answer: 'Digestivi (after-dinner bitters); the Milanese bitter-orange benchmark is Ramazzotti (Milan, 1815), with Campari the Milanese aperitivo pole. Averna (Sicily) and Montenegro (Bologna) are other styles.' Accept: 'digestivo ramazzotti', 'digestif ramazzotti', 'digestivo campari'. Remove averna and montenegro as answers to the Milanese part.
findings.verifyReason:
The finding holds. The stem asks for "one benchmark for bitter-orange Milanese style". The model answer puts "Ramazzotti/Averna (dark)" side by side and names Montenegro as a second style, which tells the student that Averna and Montenegro are Milanese benchmarks. They are not. Averna has been made in Caltanissetta, Sicily, since 1868. Montenegro was first made in 1885 by Cobianchi in Bologna and is still produced at San Lazzaro di Savena, near Bologna. Ramazzotti is the real Milanese benchmark: it was first made in Milan in 1815, and its main botanicals include Sicilian orange peel, which fits the "bitter-orange" wording. Campari is a Milanese bitter, and its orange-driven profile makes it the aperitivo pole.

The accept list makes this worse. I checked the grader in core.js. Because of its whole-word and core-phrase rules, "digestif bitter" or "digestif bitter liqueur" gets full credit without naming any Milanese benchmark. "averna montenegro campari" also passes. So a student who answers the Milanese part wrongly still gets the mark.

The proposed fix is correct. The new answer string grades itself, because core.js line 72 always accepts the displayed answer. The accept phrases "digestivo ramazzotti" and "digestif ramazzotti" match as whole phrases. One small point, which does not change the ruling: "digestivo campari" is a slightly odd accept, because Campari is an aperitivo, not a digestivo. It is harmless, since Campari is Milanese and bitter-orange-led.
findings.finalFix: Answer: "Digestivi (after-dinner bitters); the Milanese bitter-orange benchmark is Ramazzotti (Milan, 1815), with Campari the Milanese aperitivo pole. Averna (Sicily) and Montenegro (Bologna) are other styles." Accept: "digestivo ramazzotti", "digestif ramazzotti", "digestivo campari". Remove "digestivo averna montenegro campari ramazzotti" and "digestif bitter liqueur", so that neither Averna, Montenegro nor a generic answer earns credit for the Milanese part.

question.q: Amaro's role in the modern somm bar, and one benchmark for bitter-orange Milanese style:
question.ans: Digestivi; e.g., Ramazzotti/Averna (dark), Montenegro (floral), Campari the aperitivo pole

findings.because: Hanzell's 1953 Chardonnay was the Wente clone, a California selection. The cuttings came through Stony Hill, which took them from Wente's Livermore vineyard in 1948. The Pinot Noir was the Martin Ray clone. What made Hanzell Burgundian was the winemaking: Brad Webb's small French oak barrels, induced malolactic and temperature-controlled stainless steel. The clones were not Burgundian.
findings.fix: Hanzell (planted 1953) brought Burgundian winemaking to California, with small French oak barrels and induced malolactic, using Wente-clone Chardonnay by way of Stony Hill; the 'new California' movement circled back to them.
findings.verifyReason: The explanation says "Hanzell planted Burgundian clones in 1953", and that is wrong. Hanzell's 1953 Chardonnay was the Wente clone, a California heritage selection. It reached Hanzell through the McCreas' Stony Hill vineyard, which took its cuttings from Wente's Livermore vineyard in 1948. The Pinot Noir came from Martin Ray estate cuttings, now called the Mount Eden clone. Both vines were California selections. They were not clones brought in from Burgundy. The Mount Eden Pinot has a legend of a Burgundian ancestor, but that does not save the claim, and the Chardonnay, which is what this question is about, has no Burgundy link at all. What was Burgundian about Hanzell was its aim and its winemaking. James Zellerbach was among the first in California to use French oak barrels, and he paired them with temperature-controlled stainless-steel tanks. His winemaker Brad Webb is widely credited with inducing malolactic fermentation; I did not reopen a source for that point, but the fix does not depend on it. The keyed answer, the classicist restrained Chardonnay lineage, is not in dispute. Only the explanation needs correcting. The examiner's fix is accurate and matches the sources I opened.
findings.finalFix: exp: "Hanzell (planted 1953) brought Burgundian winemaking to California, with small French oak barrels and induced malolactic, using Wente-clone Chardonnay by way of Stony Hill; the 'new California' movement circled back to them."

question.q: Hanzell, Stony Hill and Mayacamas represent which stylistic lineage?
question.ans: California's classicist Chardonnay lineage — restrained, long-lived, lightly oaked
question.exp: Hanzell planted Burgundian clones in 1953; the 'new California' movement circled back to them.

question.q: AOC Alsace Grand Cru caps yields well below the regional appellation. Its base yield is:
question.exp: Alsace Grand Cru is set at 55 hl/ha, against 80 hl/ha for white AOC Alsace, with Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles lower still. The number is worth carrying because it is the heart of the case against the system: 55 hl/ha is generous for a top tier, the serious growers work at half of it voluntarily, and the law does not oblige anyone to. A hierarchy that does not bite on yield is a hierarchy the market is entitled to distrust.

findings.claim: Alsace has a trio of grand crus permitted to grow non-noble white varieties by exception.
findings.because: Under the cahier des charges, Kaefferkopf may use only Gewurztraminer, Riesling, Pinot Gris and the Muscats, all noble, alone or blended. Its exception is blending, not non-noble grapes. Only Zotzenberg (Sylvaner) and Altenberg de Bergheim (Chasselas and Pinot Blanc as accessory varieties in blends, vines planted before 26 March 2005) admit non-noble whites. Read as written, the stem makes the accepted answer 'kaefferkopf' wrong. The model answer itself treats Kaefferkopf as a blend exception.
findings.fix: Alsace has a trio of grand crus that bend the single-noble-variety rule by exception (Sylvaner, or field blends). Name any one.
findings.verifyReason:
The finding holds. I extracted the text of the Alsace grand cru cahier des charges (INAO, procédure nationale d'opposition, CNAOC of 11 Sept 2024), section V.1.

Kaefferkopf (V.1.d) is made either from a single one of gewurztraminer, pinot gris or riesling, or from a blend. In the blend, gewurztraminer is the principal variety, riesling the complementary one, and the accessory varieties are the three muscats and pinot gris. All of these are noble, and the historical section (line ~1999) confirms it.

Only two grand crus admit non-noble whites:
- Zotzenberg (V.1.c) admits sylvaner as a single variety.
- Altenberg de Bergheim (V.1.b) admits chasselas and pinot blanc as accessory varieties in blends, for vines planted before 26 March 2005.

So the stem, read as written ("permitted to grow non-noble white varieties"), makes the accepted answer "kaefferkopf" wrong, while the model answer itself treats Kaefferkopf as a blend exception. The trio is real only as "exceptions to the single-noble-variety rule for white wine."

The examiner's fix is close but needs two changes:
1. "Field blends" is not the legal term. The cahier speaks of an assemblage, with conformity judged across all of the grower's parcels, so "blends" is the accurate word.
2. Red Pinot Noir grand crus (Hengst, Kirchberg de Barr, Vorbourg) also bend the noble-variety rule. The stem therefore has to say "white" or "trio" is ambiguous.

The accept list (zotzenberg, altenberg de bergheim, kaefferkopf) and the model answer are fine once the stem is fixed.
findings.finalFix: For white wine, Alsace has a trio of grand crus that are exceptions to the single-noble-variety rule: one admits Sylvaner, and two admit blends. Name any one.

question.q: Alsace has a trio of grand crus permitted to grow non-noble white varieties by exception. Name any one.
question.exp: The noble-grape rule bends here — and separately, Pinot Noir now makes red Alsace Grand Cru at Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr (from 2022), joined by Vorbourg in 2024.
